(CNN) -- Legendary singer/songwriter Aretha Franklin sang "My Country 'Tis of Thee" at the inauguration Tuesday. Aretha Franklin says cold weather affected her voice during her performance at the inauguration on Tuesday. CNN's Larry King talks with "The Queen of Soul" about the reality of the nation's first black president, singing at the inauguration and the much-talked-about hat she wore. Larry King: Where'd you get that hat? Aretha Franklin: Well, I bought it at a little millinery that I frequent out in Detroit. King: What was that like for you (Tuesday)? Franklin: Oh. What a tremendous, mammoth morning, evening, the ball, everything, from one event to the other, was just too much. King: How did you find out you were singing? Franklin: My agent called me and he told me that he had received an invitation and a telephone call, asking for my presence and performance at the swearing-in and the inauguration. King: Did you choose the song? Franklin: Yes, I did. King: Is that a tough song to sing? Franklin: No, not at all, but (Tuesday) it was. Mainly because of the temperature outside. I don't have to tell you, it was freezing, if you were there. Some singers it doesn't bother, and others it does. I don't care for it. It affected my voice.  Watch Franklin sing at inauguration » . King: You sang at Martin Luther King's funeral. What do you remember about that? Franklin: There were very, very long lines, of course. I recall walking in the street behind the bier, somewhere maybe about 200, 300 feet from the bier, I think. I recall Leontyne Price being there, as well as Eartha Kitt. They shuttled us from one point to the other. The passing of a great man was at hand. King: How did you feel yesterday about seeing a young black man elected president? Franklin: Oh boy, how do you put it into words? There's a love affair going on with the country and Barack. I think it's the age of Barack. People have just fallen head over heels in love with him. His ascent to the presidency was miraculous. But we have to remember that he's not going to work miracles right off the top. It's going to take time.  Watch Franklin discuss joy of seeing nation's first black president » . (There's) a lot of problems, and there's a plethora of things to deal with for he and his administration. King: One thing, with your magnificent voice, is it hard to sing outdoors? Franklin: It depends on the temperature. Yesterday, Mother Nature was not very kind to me. I'm going to deal with her when I get home. It, by no means, was my standard. I was not happy with it, but I just feel blessed because it could have been five above zero or five below zero like it is in Detroit. I was still blessed to be able to pretty much just sing the melody, but I wasn't happy with it, of course. King: It was great to listen to. Franklin: I was delighted and thrilled to be there. That was the most important thing, not so much the performance, but just to be there and to see this great man go into office -- the promise of tomorrow coming to pass.

outputs.L1:
**(CNN) —** Legendary singer-songwriter Aretha Franklin performed “My Country, ’Tis of Thee” at Tuesday’s inauguration. Franklin said the cold weather affected her voice during the performance.

CNN’s Larry King spoke with the “Queen of Soul” about the historic inauguration of the nation’s first Black president, her performance, and the much-discussed hat she wore.

**Larry King:** Where did you get that hat?

**Aretha Franklin:** Well, I bought it at a little millinery that I frequent in Detroit.

**King:** What was Tuesday like for you?

**Franklin:** Oh, what a tremendous, mammoth day—from the morning and evening to the ball and everything in between. Going from one event to another was almost too much.

**King:** How did you find out you would be singing?

**Franklin:** My agent called and told me he had received an invitation and a telephone call requesting my presence and a performance at the swearing-in and inauguration.

**King:** Did you choose the song?

**Franklin:** Yes, I did.

**King:** Is it a difficult song to sing?

**Franklin:** No, not at all—but on Tuesday, it was, mainly because of the temperature outside. If you were there, I don’t have to tell you that it was freezing. The cold does not bother some singers, but it affects others. I don’t care for it; it affected my voice.

*Watch Franklin sing at the inauguration »*

**King:** You sang at Martin Luther King Jr.’s funeral. What do you remember about that?

**Franklin:** There were very, very long lines, of course. I remember walking in the street behind the bier, perhaps 200 or 300 feet away. I also recall Leontyne Price and Eartha Kitt being there. They shuttled us from one point to another. The passing of a great man was at hand.

**King:** How did you feel yesterday, seeing a young Black man elected president?

**Franklin:** Oh, boy—how do you put it into words? There is a love affair between the country and Barack. I think this is the age of Barack. People have fallen head over heels in love with him. His ascent to the presidency was miraculous.

But we must remember that he is not going to perform miracles immediately. It will take time.

*Watch Franklin discuss the joy of seeing the nation’s first Black president »*

There are many problems and a plethora of issues for him and his administration to address.

**King:** With your magnificent voice, is it difficult to sing outdoors?

**Franklin:** It depends on the temperature. Yesterday, Mother Nature was not very kind to me. I’m going to deal with her when I get home.

The performance was by no means up to my standard. I was not happy with it, but I still feel blessed because it could have been five degrees above zero—or five below, as it is in Detroit. I was fortunate to be able to sing the melody reasonably well, but of course, I was not satisfied with the performance.

**King:** It was wonderful to hear.

**Franklin:** I was delighted and thrilled to be there. That was the most important thing—not so much the performance, but simply being there and seeing this great man take office: the promise of tomorrow coming to pass.
outputs.L2:
(CNN) — At Tuesday’s presidential inauguration, iconic singer-songwriter Aretha Franklin performed “My Country ’Tis of Thee.” She later said the frigid outdoor conditions had an impact on her voice.

In an interview with CNN’s Larry King, the “Queen of Soul” reflected on performing at the ceremony, witnessing the inauguration of the country’s first Black president and wearing the hat that drew widespread attention.

King first asked where Franklin had found the hat. She explained that she purchased it from a small millinery shop in Detroit that she regularly visits.

Asked what Tuesday’s experience had been like, Franklin described the entire occasion—from the morning ceremony to the evening and the ball—as enormous and overwhelming, with one major event following another.

Franklin said she learned about the invitation through her agent. He called to tell her that he had received both an invitation and a phone call requesting that she attend and perform at the swearing-in and inauguration.

She confirmed that she personally selected “My Country ’Tis of Thee.” Although she ordinarily did not consider it a difficult song, she said it was challenging that day because of the freezing temperature. Cold weather affects some vocalists more than others, she noted, and she does not sing well in such conditions. The temperature, she said, altered her voice.

Franklin also spoke about singing at Martin Luther King Jr.’s funeral. She remembered extremely long lines and recalled walking in the street behind the bier, perhaps 200 to 300 feet away. Leontyne Price and Eartha Kitt were also present, she said, and participants were transported from one location to another. Above all, Franklin remembered that the nation was confronting the death of a great man.

When King asked how she felt about seeing a young Black man become president, Franklin said the emotion was difficult to express. She described a national “love affair” with Barack Obama and called the period “the age of Barack,” saying people had fallen deeply in love with him. His rise to the presidency seemed miraculous to her.

At the same time, Franklin cautioned that Obama would not be able to produce immediate miracles. His administration faced a great many problems and an abundance of issues, she said, and solving them would require time.

Returning to her performance, King asked whether outdoor singing was especially difficult for someone with her remarkable voice. Franklin answered that it depended on the weather. She joked that Mother Nature had treated her poorly the previous day and that she intended to settle the matter when she returned home.

Franklin said the performance did not meet her usual standard and that she was dissatisfied with it. Still, she felt fortunate because the temperature could have been five degrees above or below zero, as it can be in Detroit. Despite the cold, she was able to sing most of the melody, though she remained unhappy with the result.

King told her the performance had sounded wonderful. Franklin responded that she was delighted and excited simply to have been present. For her, the quality of the performance mattered less than being there to watch Obama take office and witness the promise of the future become reality.

Aretha Franklin spoke with CNN’s Larry King about performing at Barack Obama’s presidential inauguration and witnessing a defining moment in American history. The Queen of Soul sang “My Country, ’Tis of Thee” during the ceremony, a selection she felt was especially appropriate for the occasion.

Franklin acknowledged that the bitterly cold weather in Washington affected her performance. The freezing temperatures made it difficult for her voice to function as it normally would, she explained, and she was not entirely satisfied with how she sounded. Even so, the challenges of singing outdoors did not diminish the significance of being part of the event.

Her distinctive gray felt hat, decorated with an oversized bow and sparkling details, also became one of the inauguration’s most memorable images. Franklin discussed the attention it received after the ceremony, when it quickly became a fashion sensation and an enduring symbol of the day.

More important to Franklin, however, was what Obama’s inauguration represented. She described the atmosphere as a monumental national celebration, marked by extraordinary excitement and deep public affection for the new president. The enormous crowds and their enthusiasm demonstrated how profoundly many Americans had invested their hopes in Obama’s leadership.

Franklin also reflected on the historic importance of seeing the nation’s first Black president take office. For her, the inauguration was not simply a political transition but a major racial milestone—one that showed how far the United States had come and carried powerful meaning for Black Americans in particular. Despite the cold and the strain on her voice, she regarded her participation as an honor and the day itself as an unforgettable chapter in American history.
outputs.L5: CNN has often celebrated the life and legacy of the legendary Aretha Franklin, the undisputed “Queen of Soul.” With her powerful voice, emotional depth, and unforgettable songs such as “Respect” and “Think,” Aretha transformed popular music and became a symbol of strength and equality. Her influence reached far beyond the stage, inspiring generations of artists and supporting the civil rights movement. Through documentaries, interviews, and tributes, CNN has helped preserve the story of a legendary performer whose music continues to resonate around the world.
